bug_description.original: Heap-buffer-overflow in mg_mqtt_next_prop OSS-Fuzz report: https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=482698892 Crash type: Heap-buffer-overflow READ 1 Crash state: mg_mqtt_next_prop fuzz.c
bug_description.normalized: The staged 130-byte PoC is accepted by `mg_mqtt_parse(data, size, 5, &mm)` as an MQTT 5 PUBLISH packet with remaining length 127, empty topic, QoS 1 packet id `0x2020`, and a properties section whose encoded size byte is `0x20`. The first property byte at offset 8 is `0x09`, which Mongoose classifies as `MQTT_PROP_TYPE_BINARY_DATA`. In vulnerable `mg_mqtt_next_prop()`, the binary-data branch checks only that the two-byte length field exists, then parses bytes 9-10 (`0x20 0x20`) as `prop->val.len == 0x2020` and sets `prop->val.buf` to offset 11 without validating that 8224 bytes remain before `end`. Because the function still returns a positive next offset, the fuzz target treats the property as valid and calls `mg_crc32(0, prop.val.buf, prop.val.len)`. `mg_crc32()` then advances byte-by-byte off the end of the 130-byte PoC buffer until ASAN reports the first one-byte heap-buffer-overflow read at the buffer end.

source.description: First project parser statement that materializes the accepted MQTT packet extent from attacker-controlled header bytes. `mg_mqtt_next_prop()` later derives its `end` pointer from this exact datagram length.
source.value_from: The PoC starts with `0x3a 0xff 0x00`: byte 0 selects MQTT PUBLISH with QoS 1, and remaining-length bytes 1-2 decode to 127. After `end = p + n`, this statement records `m->dgram.len == 130`, which matches ASAN's 130-byte allocated region for `/gt/poc`.

sink.description: Crash sink inside the CRC loop. The immediately preceding dereference `uint8_t b = *(uint8_t *) buf++;` reads from the unchecked property-value pointer until it reaches the first byte past the 130-byte PoC buffer.

root_cause.description: The `MQTT_PROP_TYPE_BINARY_DATA` branch trusts the attacker-declared 16-bit payload length and advances `new_pos` without checking that `i + 2 + prop->val.len` stays below `end`. The fix adds that missing payload bound check before returning the property.

tainted_value_origin.description: PoC bytes 9-10 are both `0x20`, so this statement pair materializes the sink-driving values `prop->val.len == 8224` and `prop->val.buf == msg->dgram.buf + 11` directly from attacker-controlled property bytes.

parser_admitted.description: Sample-specific MQTT5 properties gate. The staged PoC reaches this continuation because the packet is parsed as MQTT 5 PUBLISH and still has bytes left after the topic and QoS packet id, so the parser enters the MQTT5 properties block.

coarse_trace.summary: The MQTT 5 parser accepts the PoC as a PUBLISH packet, fixes the datagram extent at 130 bytes, and records the properties-section size and start offset used by property iteration.

Property iteration starts at the first property byte, dispatches property id `0x09` to the binary-data branch, and parses a claimed length of `0x2020` without checking that the payload fits inside the packet.
Because `mg_mqtt_next_prop()` returns a positive offset and populates `prop.val`, the fuzz target passes the unchecked pointer/length pair to `mg_crc32()`, which reads past the end of the PoC buffer.

fine_trace.note: The fixed-header remaining-length varint from PoC bytes 1-2 (`0xff 0x00`) decodes to 127, so this statement fixes the accepted datagram span at 130 bytes. `mg_mqtt_next_prop()` later computes its `end` pointer from this exact extent.
At byte 7 the PoC encodes MQTT5 properties length `0x20`, so `decode_varint()` materializes `m->props_size == 32` for the later property walker.
After decoding the one-byte property-size varint, the parser records that the first property starts at offset 8. In the staged PoC, byte 8 is `0x09`.

fine_trace.code:
uint8_t *i = (uint8_t *) msg->dgram.buf + msg->props_start + ofs;
uint8_t *end = (uint8_t *) msg->dgram.buf + msg->dgram.len;
fine_trace.note: On the first iteration `ofs == 0`, so `i` points to property byte 8 and `end` points one byte past byte 129. These pointers define the actual packet window that the branch should enforce.

The byte at offset 8 is `0x09`, so `prop->id` becomes 9 and `mqtt_prop_type_by_id()` selects the `MQTT_PROP_TYPE_BINARY_DATA` branch, the branch that lacks a payload-length bound check in vulnerable code.

The only branch-local guard checks that the two-byte length field itself exists. It passes for this PoC because bytes 9-10 are present, but it does not test whether the declared binary payload also fits before `end`.

Root cause. Bytes 9-10 are `0x20 0x20`, so the branch sets `prop->val.len` to `0x2020` (8224) and `prop->val.buf` to byte 11, then advances `new_pos` as though that many bytes were valid. Unlike the string branches, this case performs no `i + 2 + prop->val.len > end` check before returning the property.

Because `mg_mqtt_next_prop()` returned a positive offset, the loop body treats the property as valid and passes the unchecked `(prop.val.buf, prop.val.len)` pair to `mg_crc32()`. For this PoC that means starting at byte 11 with declared length 8224 even though only 119 bytes remain inside the 130-byte packet.

The CRC loop runs `while (len--)` and dereferences `*(uint8_t *) buf++` each iteration. Since the caller supplied `len == 8224` for a pointer with only 119 valid bytes left, the loop eventually performs the first one-byte read at `0x50d000000192`, exactly one byte past ASAN's 130-byte PoC buffer.

sanitizer_ground_truth.source: Stage 01 reproduction_report.json, sanitizer_trace.txt, default_crash_trace.txt, patch.diff, staged vulnerable source, and the saved witness PoC bytes.

cross_validation.sink_matches_crash: Yes. The Stage 01 ASAN report records a one-byte read at the end of the 130-byte PoC buffer, and the traced sink is the `mg_crc32()` loop that repeatedly dereferences the unchecked property pointer until it reaches that exact boundary.
cross_validation.root_cause_matches_allocation_context: Yes. The root cause is the unchecked MQTT binary-property length in `mg_mqtt_next_prop()`, and the resulting over-read walks off the same harness-owned 130-byte input buffer that ASAN reports.
cross_validation.trace_consistent_with_stack: Yes. The public crash state names `mg_mqtt_next_prop` and `fuzz.c`; the patch adds the missing binary-data bound check in `mg_mqtt_next_prop()`, and the traced caller/sink path is `mg_mqtt_next_prop` -> `LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput` line 70 -> `mg_crc32`.
cross_validation.tainted_value_reaches_sink: Yes. PoC bytes 9-10 become `prop->val.len == 8224` in `mg_mqtt_next_prop()`, that unchecked length and derived pointer are passed at `test/fuzz.c:70`, and `mg_crc32()` consumes them in the crashing loop.

poc.trigger: Feed the exact staged 130-byte testcase to the `fuzz` target so `mg_mqtt_parse(data, size, 5, &mm)` accepts it as an MQTT 5 PUBLISH packet with properties size `0x20`, then `mg_mqtt_next_prop()` parses the first property as id `0x09` with binary length `0x2020`. The function returns `prop.val.buf` at byte 11 and `prop.val.len == 8224`, after which the harness calls `mg_crc32(0, prop.val.buf, prop.val.len)` and ASAN reports the read one byte past the PoC buffer.

format.name: MQTT 5 PUBLISH packet
format.contract: The witnessed trigger is this exact layout: byte 0 `0x3a` (PUBLISH, QoS 1), bytes 1-2 `0xff 0x00` (remaining length 127), bytes 3-4 `0x00 0x00` (empty topic), bytes 5-6 `0x20 0x20` (packet id), byte 7 `0x20` (properties size 32), byte 8 `0x09` (Correlation Data, parsed as `MQTT_PROP_TYPE_BINARY_DATA`), bytes 9-10 `0x20 0x20` (declared binary length 8224), and all remaining bytes `0x20`. The contract proven here is this exact binary-length mismatch, not a generalized range of MQTT property values.
